L0@P0: On arithmetic curves in the moduli spaces of curves
L1@P0: Pierre Lochak
L2@P0: 1. Introduction
L3@P0: In this paper we argue, using concrete examples, that Thurston’s viewpoint on the topology of surfaces and its subsequent ramifications are quite relevant when trying to explore the landscape delineated
L4@P0: in Grothendieck’s Esquisse d’un programme. A salient feature of Thurston’s work and legacy in this area
L5@P0: is the recognition of the importance of Teichmuller ¨ space, an essentially analytic object, in these a priori
L6@P0: topological matters; one can take as a starting point the fact that the mapping class group, defined as the
L7@P0: group of isotopy classes of diffeomorphisms of a surface, coincides with the isometry group of the corresponding Teichmuller ¨ space endowed with the Teichmuller ¨ metric. This classical result of Royden enables
L8@P0: one to bridge the gap between topology and analysis. Here we try and go one step further, moving into the
L9@P0: arithmetic nature of certain objects (old and new). Actually the intermediate step, namely from analytic to
L10@P0: algebraic geometry, will turn out to be a source of beautiful and difficult problems.
L11@P0: We will be mostly interested here in finding and studying curves which are immersed in the moduli spaces
L12@P0: of curves, are geodesic for the associated Teichmuller ¨ metric and can be defined by algebraic equations with
L13@P0: coefficients in numberfields. Some higher dimensional loci will also naturally come in. In particular we
L14@P0: isolate two classes of curves of rather different natures. The first kind we call origamis because they can be
L15@P0: defined in a purely topological and in fact combinatorial way by assembling squares of paper into a closed
L16@P0: topological surface. A particular form of origamis was defined by W.Thurston in his famous announcement
L17@P0: on his work on diffeomorphisms of surfaces ([T]) and they were taken up by W.Veech in [V1]. We show here
L18@P0: that they carry amazing arithmetic information, which we are certainly not able to decode yet, by showing
L19@P0: that they are defined by equations with coefficients sitting in certain numberfields. From now on we will call
L20@P0: an object ‘arithmetic’ if it can be defined over a numberfield. In some sense that property makes origamis
L21@P0: into a natural higher dimensional analog of the so-called ‘dessins d’enfants’. In order to prevent possible
L22@P0: misunderstandings, we note that curves sitting inside moduli spaces of curves generate an incredibly rich
L23@P0: structure, with three types of arithmetics at work which one might call modular (Riemann), period (Jacobi)
L24@P0: and hyperbolic (Fuchs) arithmetics. For elliptic curves they correspond respectively to the j and τ functions
